unit.title: Maintain quality systems within a team

summary: This unit teaches you to keep a quality system working in your team. You will learn what a quality management system is and how its documents fit together, how to control documents, records and measuring equipment, and how inspection and test plans, sampling and traceability work. You will also learn to handle non-conforming work, take part in audits, use quality data and improvement tools, and lead a team that reports faults and keeps improving.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). **Quality** means meeting the requirements every time: the drawing, the welding procedure, the code, and what the customer was promised. A **quality management system (QMS)** is the organised way a business plans, does, checks and improves its work so that it meets those requirements, not by luck or by one good welder.

At Level 3 you lead a team, and the team leader is where the quality system meets the shop floor. Managers write the policy and the procedures; you make sure your team works to them, keeps honest records, reports faults and helps to improve the way the work is done.

**Who it is for:** Welding Level 3 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres who lead or will lead a welding and fabrication team, and anyone who keeps inspection records, handles faulty work or takes part in audits.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Say what it is for, how its documents fit together, what the quality policy and objectives are, and what your part is.
Make sure only current, approved documents are in use; keep records complete, honest, secure and for the required time.
Keep tools on the register and in calibration, check them before use, and act when one is found to be wrong.
Follow the inspection and test plan, hold and witness points, sampling rules, receiving inspection and traceability.
Identify, tag and quarantine it; raise an NCR; get the disposition decided; find the root cause; check the corrective action works.
Prepare your area, show objective evidence, answer honestly and act on the findings.
Collect data on check sheets, draw Pareto charts and fishbone diagrams, read control charts, work out rates, and use PDCA.
Train, brief and involve the team; build a culture where faults are reported; handle customer feedback and complaints.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the quality system, documents, records, calibration, inspection, non-conformance, audits, improvement tools, customers and team leadership, with some percentage sums.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms) and longer answers that explain how you would handle a quality situation.

**Practical tasks**: as a group, carry out an internal audit of a workshop area against a procedure and plan corrective actions; and run quality control on a batch of welded parts (check the tools, inspect, record, draw a Pareto chart, raise an NCR and find the root cause).

blocks.note: Short-answer questions ask for exact terms such as inspection and test plan (ITP), concession, quarantine, non-conformity, fishbone diagram, quality assurance, certification body, ISO 9001, calibration certificate, self-inspection and complaints register.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Point
Quality assurance (QA)
Quality control (QC)
rows: Testing (for example dye penetrant or bend tests)
Are we set up to get it right?
Did this part come out right?

blocks.p: Both are needed. Inspection alone finds faults after the time and steel have been spent; a good system stops most of them happening.

blocks.h: The documents of a quality system

blocks.p: Quality documents are usually arranged in levels, from the short policy at the top to the many records at the bottom:

head: Level
Document
What it does
Example
rows: Management's short, signed statement of its commitment to quality and to improving
"We will supply welded products that meet our customers' requirements and the codes we work to, and we will keep improving."
Describes the whole system and how its parts link
Say who does what, and when, for each key process
Control of welding consumables; inspection; non-conforming product
Setting up the rod oven; measuring a fillet weld
Forms are blanks; filled in, they become records that prove what was done

blocks.note: A **document** says what to do, and can be revised. A **record** shows what was done, and must never be changed afterwards.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Objectives turn the policy into measurable targets. Write them SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

head: Weak objective
SMART objective
rows: Cut the weld repair rate on frame jobs from 5% to 3% of joints by 30 June
Answer every complaint within 2 working days, and close 90% within 30 days, this year
Have no measuring tool in use past its calibration date at any audit this year

ul: **ISO 9001** is the best-known international standard for quality management systems. It says what a system must do (control documents, deal with faults, audit, review, improve), not exactly how.
**ISO 3834** sets quality requirements for fusion welding, and the **AWS codes** set requirements for welding procedures, welder qualification and inspection on the jobs they cover.

**Certification** means an independent **certification body** has audited the system and found that it meets the standard. It issues a certificate and comes back for regular surveillance audits to keep it. Having a copy of the standard, or a manager's letter, is not certification.

blocks.note: The Bureau of Standards Jamaica (BSJ) publishes Jamaican standards and adopts many international ones. Government agencies and large clients may ask a fabricator for evidence of its quality system, its welder qualifications and its inspection records before giving it a contract.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Kind of cost
Examples
rows: Training, qualified procedures, planning, maintaining the rod oven
Internal failure (found before the job leaves)
Complaints, repairs on site, lost customers, a damaged name

blocks.p: Money spent on prevention usually saves much more on failures, and failures found by the customer cost the most.

ul: Make sure the team has the **current documents**, knows the procedures and follows them.
Make sure measuring tools are **in calibration** and checked before use.
Make sure inspections are done and **records** filled in honestly and on time.
Make sure faults are **reported, tagged, kept apart and recorded**.
Pass problems and ideas up through the system.
Train new members, lead by example, and take part in audits openly.
You do not have to do every inspection yourself: you make sure the system works in your area.

blocks.p: Document control makes sure **everyone works to the current, approved version** of each procedure, work instruction, WPS and drawing. A welder working to an old revision makes a part that was right last month and wrong now.

ul: Each controlled document carries a number, a title, a **revision** (letter or number), a date, the approver's name or signature, and page numbers (page 2 of 5).
A **master list** (document register) shows the current revision of every document and where each copy is kept.
A change is requested, reviewed and **approved by the person given that authority** in the system before it is issued, and the reason is recorded.
When a new revision is issued, the old copies are collected and destroyed or stamped SUPERSEDED. One copy of the old revision is kept, clearly marked, as a record.

Controlled copies are stamped (for example CONTROLLED COPY No. 3) or held on the system. Photocopies and printouts are **uncontrolled**: mark them UNCONTROLLED, CHECK REVISION BEFORE USE, or do not allow them in the workshop.
Documents from outside are controlled too: codes, client specifications and drawings, makers' manuals and safety data sheets.
Electronic documents live in one agreed place, read-only for most users, with the version history kept.

flow: A changed document arrives
Collect the old copies from the workshop
Put the new ones in their place
Brief the team on what changed and why
Check they understand
Record the briefing
Check whether work in progress is affected

blocks.note: Never mark up a controlled document with your own change, and do not let your team do it. If a WPS or work instruction seems wrong, or could be better, raise it through the system. Until the change is approved, work to the current version, or stop and ask.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Record
What it proves
rows: The work was checked and passed
Who welded which joint, to which WPS
The right materials and consumables were used, and can be traced
Calibration certificates and the equipment register
The people were competent for their tasks
Rod oven logs and consumable issue sheets
Consumables were stored and issued correctly
Faults were handled and their causes removed
Audit reports and management review minutes
The system was checked and improved
Customer problems were logged, investigated and answered

ul: Fill records in **at the time** of the work, in ink, legibly, signed and dated.

To correct an entry, draw **one line** through it so it can still be read, write the right value beside it, and initial and date the change. No correction fluid, no writing over figures, no tearing out pages.
Never fill in gaps later from memory. A missing entry is reported and dealt with, not hidden: a back-filled record is a false record.
Keep records for the **time set in the system or the contract**; structural and pressure work often needs records kept for many years.
Store paper records safe from damp, fire and termites. Keep electronic records in the agreed system, with **access controls** (passwords and permissions) and **regular backups** kept somewhere else.
Keep personal details, such as training and medical notes, confidential, as the data protection law and the Centre's rules require.

blocks.note: Heat, humidity, dust and termites destroy paper fast. Keep records in closed files in the office, not on the shop floor, and scan important ones into the agreed system.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: An inspection is only as good as the tool used. **Calibration** compares a tool's readings with a known standard and records the error; the tool is then adjusted, if it can be, or taken out of use.

ul: Every measuring and test item has an **ID number** and is listed on the register with its description, serial number, location or user, **calibration interval**, last calibration date, next due date and status.
A **label** on the item shows its ID and the date it is next due.

The **calibration certificate** gives the results, the standard used and the date. The standard must itself be checked against a higher standard, back to national or international standards: this unbroken chain is called **traceability**. A certificate without it proves very little.

Calibration is done by a calibration laboratory or by the Centre's competent person using reference standards such as gauge blocks, a reference tape, a reference thermometer or a calibrated clamp meter.

The **interval** (often 6 or 12 months) is set by the system and depends on how much the tool is used, how critical it is and its history. A tool that is dropped or misused is checked before it is used again.

head: Item
Typical calibration check
rows: Against a reference tape or rule
Zero, and readings against gauge blocks
Against known sizes; checked for wear and damage
Against a reference square or angle
Welding machine meters (current, voltage, wire feed speed)
Against a calibrated meter, because the WPS limits are set in amps, volts and wire speed
Against a reference thermometer; temperature-indicating crayons kept in date
Against a reference gauge or meter

ul: Check the label is in date before you use the tool.
Zero calipers and micrometers, and check for damage, wear and dirt.
Report a tool that has been dropped, or that gives odd readings, and do not use it until it has been checked.
Store tools in their cases, clean and dry.

blocks.h: When a tool is found out of calibration

flow: Take it out of use and label it
Record the error found
List all the work measured with it since its last good calibration
Decide whether the error could have let bad work pass
Re-measure the work that matters, and raise an NCR for anything that fails
Repair, adjust and recalibrate the tool, or scrap it
Find out why it went wrong (dropped, overdue, misused) and stop it happening again

blocks.note: Machine meters matter because the WPS gives current and voltage ranges. If a machine's display reads higher than the real current, a welder who sets it inside the WPS range is actually welding below it, and nobody can tell from the display.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Add the interval to the date of the last calibration. A gauge calibrated on 20 January with a 6-month interval is next due on 20 July. A tool past its due date is **out of calibration**, even if it still seems to read correctly.
The **ITP** lists every inspection and test on a job, in order: what is checked, when, by whom, against what (drawing, WPS, code), the record produced, and the kind of point.

head: Kind of point
What happens
Example
rows: Work **stops** until the inspection is done and the work released in writing
Fit-up checked before the root run; welds inspected before painting
The client or inspector is told in advance and may attend; if they do not come at the agreed time, work may go on
The client watches a weld test or a load test
Records are reviewed; nobody needs to attend

head: Stage
What is checked
rows: Materials and consumables against the order, the certificates and their condition
Drawing revision, material, WPS, welder qualification, fit-up, cleanliness, preheat where required
The first part of a batch, fully, before the rest are made
Settings against the WPS, cleaning between runs, interpass temperature where required
Sizes, weld size and profile, visible faults, finish, marking, records

ul: **Self-inspection**: the welder checks their own work before handing it on. It catches most faults early and cheaply.
**Independent inspection**: someone who did not make the part gives final acceptance. They are less likely to miss faults and are under no pressure to pass their own work.

blocks.p: When not every part can be checked, a **sample** is, for example 1 part in every 10. A batch of 150 at 1 in 10 means 15 parts are checked.

ul: The sampling plan says how many to check and what to do when a sample fails.

When a sample finds faults, the **whole batch is suspect**: stop, keep the batch apart, check more of it or all of it, and find the cause. Throwing away the faulty samples and sending the rest is never acceptable.
Steel and consumables are bought from an **approved supplier list**: suppliers checked for quality, certificates, delivery and price, and their performance recorded.
On delivery, check against the purchase order and delivery note: grade, size, quantity, certificates, heat or batch numbers, and condition (damage, rust, wet or opened packets, dented tins).
Accept and book in what is right. Keep apart and label anything wrong or doubtful, record it, and tell the supplier and the store.

blocks.p: Traceability means that every weld and part can be followed back to where it came from.

flow: Steel heat number, recorded on delivery and transferred to each cut part
Consumable batch number, recorded when issued
Weld number on the weld map
WPS used, welder's identity, date
Inspection and test results, repairs and NCRs for that weld
Data book handed to the client: certificates, weld map, records, as-built drawings

blocks.p: If a fault or failure is found later, traceability shows the cause (a batch of steel, a welder, a procedure) and which other parts might have the same problem, so they can be found quickly.

A **non-conformance** is any failure to meet a requirement. It may be in the product (an undersized weld, the wrong steel, a hole in the wrong place) or in the process (a step skipped, a record missing, a tool out of calibration).

flow: Identify it and stop work on it
Tag it and move it to a marked quarantine area
Raise a non-conformance report (NCR)
Get the disposition decided by an authorised person
Carry out the disposition and inspect again
Find the root cause
Agree a corrective action with an owner and a date
Check later that the action worked
Close out the NCR

ul: The job, drawing and revision
The requirement, and what was found (measurements, photos)
How many items are affected, who found it and when
The immediate action taken
The disposition and who approved it
The root cause and the corrective action, with an owner and a date
Verification that the action worked, and the close-out signature

blocks.h: Disposition: what to do with the faulty item

head: Disposition
Meaning
Example
rows: Make it **fully** meet the original requirement
Grind out an undersized weld and re-weld it to size; drill a small hole out to the right size
Make it fit for use, but **not fully** to the original requirement; needs approval, often the customer's
Plate over a hole drilled in the wrong place, to an approved method
Accept it unchanged; only with the written agreement of the customer or an authorised person (a **concession**)
A small cosmetic fault the client agrees to accept
It cannot be made acceptable; destroy or mark it so it cannot be used by mistake

blocks.note: The welder who made a faulty part, or a team leader in a hurry, cannot decide to use it as it is. Painting over a fault to hide it is never a disposition: it turns an internal failure into an external one.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The **root cause** is the cause which, if removed, stops the problem coming back. It usually lies in the system (a method, the training, a document), not just in "the welder was careless". If you only blame a person, the same fault happens again with someone else.

ul: **5 whys**: ask "why?" again and again, about five times, until you reach a cause you can fix.
**Fishbone diagram** (cause-and-effect or Ishikawa diagram): the problem at the head, and causes grouped on six bones: People, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement and Environment.

head: Why?
Answer
rows: Why were the brackets too short?
The cutting list gave the wrong length.
Why was the cutting list wrong?
It was worked out from the drawing before Revision C.
Why was the old drawing used?
The estimator's copy was not on the drawing register, so it was not replaced.
Why was it not on the register?
The procedure did not require office copies to be registered.

blocks.p: Root cause: the drawing control procedure. Corrective action: register every copy, including office copies, and check cutting lists against the current revision.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Fixing the faulty item itself (rework, repair). It deals with this item, not the cause.
Removing the cause of a problem that **has happened**, so it does not happen again
Removing the cause of a problem that **could happen**, before it does

ul: A good corrective action is specific, has an owner and a due date, and fits the cause.
Check it later with the records: has the problem come back since? Only then close it out.
Use what you learn elsewhere: could the same cause affect other jobs or teams?

blocks.p: An **internal quality audit** is a planned, independent check that the team follows its system **and** that the system works. It checks the system, not the people's private lives or their skill as welders.

head: Kind of audit
Who carries it out
rows: Trained staff from another part of the business
An independent certification body, for certification

flow: Audit plan: what will be audited, when and by whom
Checklist written from the procedure
Opening meeting with the area
Gather objective evidence: watch the work, check records, ask questions
Grade each finding
Closing meeting: explain the findings
Audit report
Corrective actions agreed, done and checked
Findings closed

head: Finding
Meaning
Example
rows: The requirement is met, with evidence
Every gauge sampled is labelled and in date
A requirement is not met and the system has broken down, or a whole part of it is missing
No calibration system at all; work shipped without the final inspection
A single lapse in a system that otherwise works
One gauge out of twenty is past its due date
Not a breach, but could become one or could be done better
Oven log kept, but hard to read

blocks.p: Grading rules vary between systems; follow the Centre's audit procedure.

**Objective evidence** is fact that can be checked: a record, a document, something seen, a measurement, or a statement that a record confirms. "We always do it" is not evidence; the signed oven log is.

head: As auditor
As the team leader being audited
rows: Audit areas you do not work in, so the audit stays fair and independent
Ask polite, open questions: "Show me how you...", "How do you know...?"
Sample records and note exactly what you saw (record number, date)
Before: read the audit plan; check records are complete, tools in date and the area tidy; brief the team to answer honestly
During: go round with the auditor, answer truthfully, show records, hide nothing
Never fill gaps in records just before an audit
After: agree what each finding means, find the root cause, agree actions with owners and dates, and show evidence they worked

blocks.note: If you disagree with a finding, say so calmly at the closing meeting and show your evidence. If the evidence does not change it, accept the finding and act on it. Arguing, blaming another department or hiding a record makes things worse.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: At set intervals, senior managers review the whole system: audit results, NCRs and corrective actions, customer feedback and complaints, quality objectives and results, supplier performance, training and resources. They decide on improvements, new objectives and resources. The data your team records feeds this review.

head: Stage
What happens
Example
rows: Define the problem with data, find the cause, plan a change and set a target
12% of MIG handrail joints need spatter ground off. Cause found: dirty nozzles. Plan: clean nozzles every hour. Target: under 4%.
Try the change, often on a small scale
One bay tries it for two weeks
Measure the results and compare them with the target
Spatter repairs fall to 5%: better, but not on target
If it worked, make it standard (update the procedure, train everyone). If not, learn and go round again
Keep hourly cleaning in all bays; next, look at the voltage setting

blocks.p: A simple form for **counting how often each kind of fault happens**: a column for each fault type, a row for each day, job or welder, and a tally mark for each fault found. Keep it simple and record honestly, or the data is worthless.

A bar chart of causes in order from **largest to smallest**, often with a line showing the running (cumulative) percentage. It shows that a few causes usually give most of the problems (the 80/20 idea), so the team works on the biggest bar first.
There were 120 faults in all. Porosity and spatter together caused 70% of them, so fixing those two first gives the biggest gain.
Write the problem at the head. The team brainstorms causes onto the six bones (People, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement, Environment), then tests the likely ones with data before acting.

head: Bone
Possible causes of porosity
rows: Welder not trained on the new wire; long arc
Leaking gas hose; faulty gas valve
Joint not cleaned; wrong torch angle
Damp electrodes; rusty or oily plate
Draughts or wind across the bay; high humidity

blocks.p: A control chart plots a result over time, such as the daily repair percentage or a fillet leg measured every hour. It has a **centre line** (the average) and **upper and lower control limits** worked out from the process's normal variation.

ul: Points scattered at random inside the limits: the process is **steady**. Do not adjust it for every small change.
A point **outside** a limit: something has changed. Find the cause.
A **pattern** inside the limits also shows a change: a long run on one side of the centre line (often 7 or more points in a row), or a steady climb or fall.
Control limits come from the process; specification limits come from the drawing or code. They are not the same thing.

head: Measure
How to work it out
Example
rows: 91% to 96% is a rise of 5 percentage points
A J$60 000 jig that saves J$15 000 of rework a month pays for itself in 4 months
5 hours × J$2 000 + J$3 000 of consumables = J$13 000

blocks.note: A rise from 91% to 96% is 5 **percentage points**. It is not a 5% rise: 5 is about 5.5% of 91. Say "points" when you compare two percentages.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Lead by example.** Follow the procedures yourself, and never say "skip it this once".
Explain **why** each check matters, with real examples of what goes wrong, so it is not just paperwork.
Involve the team in setting targets and reviewing results. Put the charts on the wall and discuss them at short, regular meetings.
Praise good work and give credit for ideas, and act on the good ones.
Treat faults as chances to learn. If people fear blame, they **hide faults**, and a hidden fault is found later by the customer at a much higher cost.
Deal fairly with deliberate rule-breaking, through the Centre's procedures.
Give people the time, tools and training to do the job right.
Keep a **training matrix**: who is trained and qualified for which procedures, WPSs, equipment and inspections.
Keep **training records**: what was trained, when, by whom, signed by the trainer and the trainee. They show each person is competent for their tasks.
Keep **welder qualification records** current, as the code the Centre works to requires.
Roll out a new or changed procedure properly: brief the team, show the method, check understanding (ask them to show you), and record the training.

blocks.h: When someone does not follow a procedure

flow: Talk to them privately and calmly
Find out why: they may not understand it, may lack time or tools, or the procedure may not work
Fix the cause: retrain, provide the tools, or raise a change to the procedure
Make clear what is expected from now on
Keep an eye on it
If it carries on, follow the Centre's disciplinary procedure and record what happened

ul: Collect **feedback**: comments at handover, short surveys, repeat orders. It shows whether the work meets customers' needs and where to improve.
Log every complaint in the **complaints register**: the customer, the job, what is wrong, the date. Thank the customer and tell them when they will hear back.
Investigate: visit, take photos, check the records for that job.
Put it right, find the root cause, and take corrective action so it does not happen again.
Tell the customer what was found and done. Close the complaint when the customer is satisfied.
Review complaints regularly for trends.

blocks.p: Example: a gate fitted in Linstead will not latch a month after it was hung. The records show the hinge post was set in concrete and the gate hung the next day, before the concrete had cured, and the post has leaned. The gate is re-hung at no charge, and the corrective action adds a minimum curing time to the installation work instruction.

blocks.note: News travels fast by word of mouth, and one unhappy customer tells many others. A complaint handled quickly, honestly and fairly often keeps the customer for life.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work through it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain what a quality management system is for, and the difference between quality assurance and quality control.
I can put the quality documents in order, from the policy down to forms and records, and say what each does.
I can tell a weak quality objective from a SMART one.
I can explain what ISO 9001 and certification mean.
I can describe the team leader's part in keeping the system working.
I can explain how document control works and what to do when a document changes.
I can keep and correct records properly, and keep them secure.
I can explain calibration, keep tools on a register, work out due dates, and act when a tool is out of calibration.
I can explain an ITP, hold and witness points, self-inspection and independent inspection.
I can work out a sample size and say what to do when a sample fails.
I can check a delivery and explain traceability from heat number to data book.
I can handle a non-conformance: tag, quarantine, NCR, disposition, root cause, corrective action, close-out.
I can tell rework, repair, use as is (concession) and scrap apart.
I can use the 5 whys and a fishbone diagram to find a root cause.
I can prepare for, take part in and respond to an internal audit, using objective evidence.
I can use PDCA, check sheets, Pareto charts and control charts.
I can work out repair rates, pass rates, percentage points, payback and failure costs.
I can build a quality culture, train the team and handle a customer complaint.

terms: Audit
A planned, independent check that a system is followed and works
Calibration
Comparing a tool's readings with a known standard and recording the error
Calibration certificate
The record of a calibration: the results, the standard used and the date
Certification body
An independent organisation that audits a quality system and issues a certificate
Check sheet
A tally form for counting how often each kind of fault happens
Complaints register
The log in which every customer complaint is recorded
Concession
Written agreement from the customer or an authorised person to use a non-conforming item as it is
Control chart
A chart of a result over time with a centre line and control limits
Corrective action
Action to remove the cause of a problem that has happened
Disposition
The decision on what to do with a non-conforming item
Document control
The system that keeps only current, approved documents in use
Fishbone diagram
A cause-and-effect diagram with causes grouped on six bones
Hold point
A stage where work must stop until it is inspected and released
ISO 9001
The best-known international standard for quality management systems
ITP
Inspection and test plan: the list of every inspection and test on a job
Non-conformance
A failure to meet a requirement
NCR
Non-conformance report: the record of a non-conformance and how it was dealt with
Objective evidence
Facts that can be checked, such as records and measurements
Pareto chart
A bar chart of causes from largest to smallest
PDCA
Plan, Do, Check, Act: the improvement cycle
Preventive action
Action to remove the cause of a problem that could happen
Quality assurance (QA)
The planned system that prevents faults
Quality control (QC)
Checking the product to find faults
Quality policy
Management's short statement of commitment to quality
Quarantine
Keeping faulty or doubtful items apart, tagged, in a marked area until a decision is made
Record
Evidence of what was done; never altered afterwards
Rework
Making a faulty item fully meet the original requirement
Root cause
The cause which, if removed, stops a problem coming back
Self-inspection
A worker checking their own work before handing it on
Traceability
Being able to follow a part or weld back to its materials, people, procedure and records
Witness point
A stage the client or inspector may attend; work may go on if they do not come

c1.title: Security doors in Spaldings
c1.text: Marlon leads a welding team at a shop in Spaldings, Clarendon, making 30 steel security doors for a housing scheme. On Monday, drawing D-112 was revised from Rev 1 to Rev 2: the hinges moved 50 mm. On Wednesday Marlon finds a Rev 1 print in a welder's locker, and six doors have already been welded. On the booth wall, a copy of WPS-04 has its current range crossed out and a new one pencilled in by Delroy, a welder, who says "it runs better". Keisha, the inspector, has written a leg length of 8 mm instead of 6 mm on an inspection sheet.

c2.title: Calibration checks at a steel shop in Bog Walk
c2.text: Mr Wint is preparing his team's tools for a structural job at a steel shop in Bog Walk, St Catherine. Today is 7 November 2026. The register shows the rod oven thermometer was last calibrated on 10 March 2026, on a 6-month interval. A digital caliper is used for checking fit-up gaps. When machine M-7's display reads 140 A, a calibrated clamp meter reads 120 A. The WPS for the root runs gives 110–130 A.

c3.title: Weld repairs at a frame yard in Hayes
c3.text: A yard in Hayes, Clarendon, makes steel frames for prefabricated houses, and its bays open on the side facing the sea breeze. In four weeks, 1 600 joints were inspected and 96 needed repair: porosity 41, undercut 22, lack of fusion 15, wrong size 10, cracks 3 and other faults 5. The target is a repair rate below 4%. The team leader also keeps a daily control chart of the repair percentage.

c4.title: Handrail posts for a hospital in Savanna-la-Mar
c4.text: A team in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, made 24 handrail posts for a hospital ramp. At final inspection, every base plate was found to have Ø18 holes instead of the Ø22 holes on the current drawing. The driller had worked from a job card that listed M16 bolts; it had been printed from the Rev 1 drawing. Opening the holes out took 6 hours at J$2 500 an hour, plus J$4 000 for a new drill and cutting fluid.

c5.title: An internal audit in Ocho Rios
c5.text: Kerry-Ann leads a welding team at a steel shop in Ocho Rios, St Ann. An auditor from the estimating office audits her team's training and welder qualification records. Eleven of the twelve welders' files are complete, but one has no continuity entry for the last eight months. A welder who started last month has no training record for WPS-02, although Kerry-Ann says she trained him on his first day.

questions.q: What should Marlon do first about the six doors already welded?
o: Send them out, as they were made before Wednesday
Set them aside, tagged, and check them to Rev 2
Move the hinges on all thirty doors to be safe
Let the welder finish them to Rev 1, as he started
questions.why: Doors that may not meet the current drawing are identified, tagged and kept apart before anything else happens. Checking them against Rev 2 shows which need rework, and an NCR records it.

questions.q: How should Marlon deal with Delroy's pencilled change on the WPS copy?
o: Accept it, since Delroy is the most experienced welder
Initial the change so that it becomes part of the WPS
Replace that copy; Delroy proposes the change formally
Leave it up until the next audit picks it up
questions.why: Only the person given that authority may change a WPS, and it may need re-qualifying. Until a change is approved, the team works to the current version; Delroy's idea goes through the system.

questions.q: How should Keisha correct the wrong leg length on her inspection sheet?
o: Cover the 8 with correction fluid and write 6 on top
Strike the 8 through once, write 6, initial and date
Copy the whole sheet out again from memory, but correctly
Write the 6 over the top of the 8 so it reads correctly
questions.why: A single line keeps the original entry readable, and the initials and date show who changed it and when. Correction fluid, overwriting and rewriting from memory all destroy the evidence a record is meant to give.

questions.q: Which corrective action best stops old prints being used again?
o: Warn the welder that he will lose a day's pay next time
Withdraw old prints via the register at each revision
Stop printing drawings and work only from a screen
Ask the welders to check with each other each morning
questions.why: The root cause is that old copies were not withdrawn. Collecting every copy listed in the register when a new revision is issued removes that cause; warnings and reminders do not.

questions.q: Is the rod oven thermometer in calibration today?
o: No: it was due on 10 September 2026
Yes: it is next due on 10 March 2027
Yes: it is next due on 10 December 2026
No: it was due on 10 June 2026
questions.why: 10 March plus 6 months is 10 September 2026, so by 7 November it is overdue and must not be used until it is calibrated again, however well it seems to work.

questions.q: What makes the clamp meter's calibration certificate good evidence of accuracy?
o: It shows the meter was bought new from an approved supplier
It shows when the meter was last used on a job in the shop
It proves the meter can never drift out of its tolerance
It gives results against standards traced to national ones
questions.why: A calibration only means something if the standard used was itself checked, in an unbroken chain, back to national or international standards. Any instrument can drift, which is why it is recalibrated at intervals.

questions.q: Before checking fit-up gaps, which check should the inspector make on the digital caliper?
o: Close the jaws, see it reads zero, and check its label date
Measure the gap twice and take the larger of the two readings
Change the battery, whether or not it is running low
Ask the last person who used it whether it was working
questions.why: Zeroing shows the caliper starts from a true zero, and the label shows it is within its calibration period. A user check takes seconds and stops a wrong reading being recorded as a pass.

questions.q: What does the difference on machine M-7 mean for the root runs?
o: They ran hotter than the welder thought
Only today's welds could be affected
They may have run below the WPS range
Nothing, as the WPS range is 20 A wide
questions.why: The display reads high (140 A shown when 120 A flows), so a welder who set 120 A on it was really welding at about 103 A, below the 110 A minimum. Welds made on M-7 since its last good check must be assessed.

questions.q: What was the repair rate over the four weeks?
questions.why: Repair rate = repairs ÷ joints inspected × 100 = 96 ÷ 1 600 × 100 = 6%. That is above the 4% target, so action is needed.

questions.q: On a Pareto chart, what share of all repairs do the two largest causes make up?
o: About 41%
About 63%
About 66%
About 22%
questions.why: Porosity (41) and undercut (22) make 63 repairs out of 96: 63 ÷ 96 × 100 ≈ 66%. Fixing these two first gives the biggest gain.

questions.q: On a fishbone diagram for porosity, under which heading does "sea breeze through the open bays" belong?
o: Method
Material
Measurement
Environment
questions.why: Wind and weather are Environment causes. A breeze can blow the shielding gas away from the weld pool, so this is a likely cause to test with data.

questions.q: The team tried windbreak screens on one bay for two weeks, and its porosity fell from 2.6% to 0.8% of joints. What is the Act step?
o: Fit screens in every bay and add them to the work instruction
Take the screens down, since the trial period is now over
Keep screens on that bay only and stop recording porosity
Start a new trial on undercut first, then decide about the screens
questions.why: When a change works, Act makes it the standard: put it in place everywhere, update the work instruction and train the team. Keep collecting data to check the gain holds.

questions.q: The last eight points on the daily chart are all above the centre line, though inside the control limits. What does this suggest?
o: Nothing, because every point is inside the limits
The centre line should be moved up to fit the points
No action until a point falls above the upper limit
The process has probably changed; look for why
questions.why: A long run on one side of the centre line is very unlikely by chance, so the process has probably shifted even though no point is outside a limit. Finding the cause early stops repairs rising further.

questions.q: Opening the holes out to Ø22 so the posts fully meet the drawing is which kind of disposition?
o: Rework
Repair
Concession
Scrap
questions.why: Rework makes an item fully meet the original requirement. A repair makes it usable but not fully to the requirement, and a concession accepts it unchanged.

questions.q: Where should the 24 posts be kept until the disposition is decided?
o: On the delivery rack, ready to go out when approved
In a marked hold area, tagged, away from good stock
In the bay where they were made, with the rest of the job
In the scrap bin, so that nobody can use them yet
questions.why: Quarantine stops faulty or doubtful items being used or sent out by mistake while a decision is made. Scrapping them would waste posts that can be reworked.

questions.q: Which corrective action deals with the root cause?
o: Tell the driller to read drawings more carefully
Buy a set of Ø22 drills to keep in every bay
Print job cards only from the current revision
Have the welders check every hole before welding
questions.why: The job card came from an old revision, so the cause lies in how job cards are produced. Tying them to the current revision on the master list stops it happening again, whoever does the drilling.

questions.q: What was the internal failure cost of the rework?
questions.why: Labour is 6 hours × J$2 500 = J$15 000; adding J$4 000 for the drill and cutting fluid gives J$19 000. It counts as internal failure because the fault was found before the posts left the shop.

questions.q: How would most auditors grade the one welder's file with no continuity entry, when the other eleven are complete?
o: As a major non-conformity
As a minor non-conformity
As a conformity
As an observation only
questions.why: A single lapse in a system that otherwise works is usually a minor non-conformity. A major one means the system has broken down or is missing; follow the Centre's own grading rules.

questions.q: Which would be objective evidence that the new welder was trained on WPS-02?
o: Kerry-Ann's word that she trained him on his first day
The new welder saying that he knows the WPS well
A training record, signed and dated at the time
A record that Kerry-Ann writes up after the audit
questions.why: Objective evidence is a fact that can be checked, made at the time. A record written afterwards is back-filling, and a statement is not evidence on its own; the missing record is the finding.

questions.q: Which of these is quality assurance rather than quality control?
o: Measuring the fillet legs on finished brackets
Dye-penetrant testing a weld after it is made
Counting rejects at final inspection each week
Training welders on a new WPS before the job
questions.why: Quality assurance is the planned system that prevents faults, such as training, procedures and calibration. Measuring, testing and counting rejects are quality control: they find faults after the work is done.
